title: Gorumara Safaris Explained: Towers, Slots and Booking
meta_description: How Gorumara safaris work: watchtowers like Jatraprasad, Medla and Chandrachur, safari slots, online booking, jeep fees, closures and what you may see.
summary: A Gorumara safari is a short jeep ride from Lataguri to one watchtower, where you sit for an hour or so over a salt lick or grassland and wait for rhinos, gaur, elephants and deer. Slots are booked through the West Bengal forest department, a six-seat jeep with fees costs ₹2,500–3,500, and the park closes from mid-June to mid-September.

sections.heading: How a Gorumara safari works
paras: Gorumara is small, about 80 km² of sal forest and riverine grassland between the Murti and Jaldhaka rivers, and it is not run like a tiger reserve where jeeps drive long loops looking for animals. Instead, each safari slot takes a jeep along a fixed forest road to one watchtower. You climb up, sit quietly for 45 minutes to an hour over a salt lick, a waterhole or a stretch of grass, and come back. The animals come to you, or they do not.

This makes Gorumara better for patient watching than for chasing sightings, and it suits families and older travellers, since the jeep rides are short and the towers have railings and roofs. It also means that the tower you book decides what you are likely to see. A safari is booked for a specific tower and a specific slot. The ticket counters for Gorumara are in Lataguri, the village on the Malbazar–Maynaguri road, and jeeps leave from near the counters.

There are usually four to five slots a day, from early morning to late afternoon, each lasting two to three hours including the drive. The first and last slots are the best, because rhinos and gaur come out to feed in the cool hours. Slot timings and the number of jeeps allowed per tower are set by the forest department and change with the season, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: What you might see
paras: The animal everyone hopes for is the Indian one-horned rhino. Gorumara's population was estimated at about 61 in the March 2025 count, small enough that rangers know many individuals by sight. Gaur, the Indian bison, are common, and herds of 20 or more come to the Chapramari waterhole and the Chandrachur salt lick in late afternoon. Asian elephants move through the park and the tea gardens around it, often in family groups.

Sambar, barking deer, spotted deer and wild boar are regular. Peafowl strut across the grass below Jatraprasad. Leopards live here but are rarely seen; there are no resident tigers. Birders should look for hornbills, woodpeckers, drongos, minivets and, in the wetlands near Chukchuki, storks and herons. A slot with nothing but deer and peacocks is common, and it is part of the deal. Two or three slots over a two-night stay give a far better chance than one.

It helps to know how hemmed in this park is. Gorumara began as a reserved forest in 1895, became a sanctuary of only about 7 km² in 1949 and a national park in 1992. Tea gardens, villages, a highway and the Dooars railway surround it, which is why elephants and gaur so often wander out at dusk, and why the watchtower system, rather than more jeeps on more roads, suits it.

sections.heading: Booking a slot
paras: Gorumara and Chapramari slots are booked through the West Bengal forest department's online booking system, which also handles Jaldapara and Buxa. The portal and its web address have changed over the years, so search for the department's official nature tourism booking site rather than trusting a link on a travel forum, and avoid look-alike sites that charge extra. Bookings usually open some weeks ahead; winter weekends, Christmas week and the Durga Puja holidays sell out first.

You book a jeep for a slot and a tower, with the names and ID numbers of all passengers, and pay the vehicle, guide and entry fees online or at the counter, depending on the system in force that season. Bring the same ID to Lataguri; it is checked. Unsold seats are released at the counter the evening before or early on the day, and queues form before the counter opens. Many homestays and resorts in Lataguri will book for you, usually for a fee of a few hundred rupees.

A six-seat jeep with fees costs roughly ₹2,500–3,500 in 2025–26, so a full jeep comes to ₹450–600 a person. Foreign nationals pay more, and video cameras carry an extra fee. All of this changes each season; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Closures and the October 2025 floods
paras: Gorumara, Chapramari and the other Dooars parks close from about 16 June to 15 September each year for the monsoon. Gorumara has also kept a weekly closure day for safaris, which has been Thursday in recent years. Individual towers and routes close when roads wash out, when elephants are aggressive or during census work.

In early October 2025, extreme rain sent the Jaldhaka, Murti and smaller rivers through the park. Forest staff recovered dead gaur, deer and at least one rhino, and some animals were swept downstream. The park closed for repairs and reopened afterwards, but some forest roads and towers may still be limited. Ask at the Lataguri counter what is running, and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Where to sleep for Gorumara
paras: Your base decides how early you can be at the counter and how quiet your evenings are.

Lataguri is the practical choice: the counters and jeep stand are here, dozens of homestays charge ₹1,200–2,000 a person with meals, and dhabas line the road. The cost is noise from the highway and from resort parties on winter weekends. Pick a homestay on a side lane, away from the main road.

Murti, 15–20 minutes away on the riverbank, is quieter, with the forest corporation's Banani cottages and tents and a few private resorts. You will need a car to the Lataguri counter, ₹600–1,000 for the trip. Dhupjhora, between Gorumara and Chapramari, has a forest corporation elephant camp where you can watch the camp elephants bathed in the river in the morning; rooms are simple and sell out early. Kalipur eco village, a small forest corporation camp inside the forest on the Lataguri side, is the most remote option, with a watchtower nearby.

Forest corporation rooms are booked on the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation's site, separately from safari slots. Book both, and check that your safari dates match your room dates, since the online systems do not talk to each other.

sections.heading: Tower etiquette and practical tips
paras: A watchtower works only if everyone on it is quiet. One group talking loudly on the stairs can empty a salt lick in minutes, and you will have paid for nothing.
list: Choose the first slot of the morning or the last of the afternoon for the best chance of rhinos and gaur.
Wear muted greens, browns and greys; avoid red, white and bright yellow.
Keep voices low, phones silent and flash off; no food packets or plastic on the towers.
Bring binoculars: animals are often 100–300 m away across the grass.
Carry a warm layer for winter dawns and water for afternoon slots in April and May.
Book two or three slots over two nights, at different towers, rather than one.

faqs.q: How do I book a Gorumara safari?
faqs.a: Through the West Bengal forest department's official online booking system, which opens some weeks ahead. You book a jeep, a slot and a tower, with the names and IDs of all passengers. Unsold seats are sold at the Lataguri counter. Homestays will book for a small fee. Portals change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which is the best watchtower in Gorumara?
faqs.a: Jatraprasad, over a salt lick and the Murti grassland, is the most popular for rhinos and gaur and sells out first. Chandrachur is quieter and good for gaur and elephants in late afternoon. Medla adds a bullock-cart ride that children love, and Chapramari, a separate sanctuary, has the biggest gaur herds.

faqs.q: How much does a Gorumara safari cost?
faqs.a: About ₹2,500–3,500 for a six-seat jeep including entry, guide and vehicle fees in 2025–26, so ₹450–600 each when the jeep is full. Foreign nationals and video cameras pay extra. Agents add a margin. Fees are revised often, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What are the Gorumara safari timings?
faqs.a: There are usually four to five slots a day from early morning to late afternoon, each lasting two to three hours with the drive. The first morning slot and the last afternoon slot give the best sightings. Exact timings change with the season and are set by the forest department.

faqs.q: Is Gorumara closed on any day of the week?
faqs.a: Gorumara has kept a weekly closure day for safaris, which has been Thursday in recent years, besides the annual monsoon closure from about 16 June to 15 September. Towers can also close after floods or for census work. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Will we definitely see a rhino in Gorumara?
faqs.a: No. Gorumara has about 61 rhinos in 80 km², and on a single slot you may see only deer, gaur and peacocks. Two or three slots at different towers over two nights improve your chances considerably. Jaldapara, with about 330 rhinos, gives better odds.

faqs.q: What is the Medla bullock-cart ride?
faqs.a: On the Medla safari, the last stretch to the watchtower is done in a bullock cart rather than the jeep, for a small extra fee of about ₹40–100 a person. The tower overlooks river grassland where rhinos and elephants feed. It is popular with families, so book early.

No. Chapramari is a separate wildlife sanctuary next to Gorumara, between the Murti and Jaldhaka, but its slots are booked through the same system and jeeps leave from the same area. Its single watchtower over a waterhole is known for the largest gaur herds in West Bengal.

faqs.q: Is Gorumara open after the October 2025 floods?
faqs.a: The park reopened after repairs following the October 2025 floods, which killed gaur, deer and at least one rhino. Some forest roads and towers may still be limited. Ask at the Lataguri counter which towers are running before you book, and check current status before you travel.
